provinces.name: Pannonia Prima
provinces.endedNote: ceded to or occupied by the Huns c. 433 (disputed)
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Pannoniae primae et Norici ripensis

phases.t: northwestern Pannonia: Savaria, Scarbantia, Carnuntum, Vindobona
Quadic and Sarmatian invasions; federate settlements after 380

provinces.summary: The western half of Upper Pannonia. Martin of Tours was born at Savaria around 316; by Ammianus' day Carnuntum was 'a deserted town'. Aetius is generally thought to have ceded Pannonian territory to the Huns around 433 in return for their support.

provinces.name: Savia (Pannonia Savensis)
provinces.endedNote: lost after the Avar arrival of 568 (date approximate)

phases.t: the Sava valley with Siscia and its mint
Ostrogothic: Cassiodorus' Variae include letters to its governor (4.49; 5.14)
contested by Lombards, Gepids and the empire; Avars after 568

provinces.summary: The Sava valley, with the mint and martyr-shrine of Siscia (Quirinus, martyred 309). Unusually, Theoderic's administration kept governing it as a Roman province, and Cassiodorus' letters deal with its tax abuses.

provinces.name: Pannonia Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Sirmium surrendered to the Avars in 582

phases.t: Sirmium an imperial residence; battles of Cibalae (316) and Mursa (351)
Hunnic capture of Sirmium (441), then Gepids
Ostrogothic, then Gepid
Roman again under Justin II; Sirmium surrendered to the Avars after a siege of 580-582

provinces.summary: Sirmium was one of the tetrarchic capitals and the birthplace of several emperors (Probus among them); Constantius II held councils there. Two of the bloodiest battles of the civil wars were fought in the province, at Cibalae (316) and Mursa (351). Its fall to the Avars in 582 broke the Danube frontier.

sources.r: fragments on the siege of Sirmium

provinces.name: Valeria (Pannonian)
provinces.endedNote: given up to the Huns c. 433 (disputed)

phases.t: named after Galerius' wife Valeria; the Danube bend with Aquincum
Quadi and Sarmatians invade (374); Valentinian I dies of a stroke while receiving Quadic envoys (375)

provinces.summary: Galerius drained Lake Pelso and cleared forests here and named the new province after his wife, Diocletian's daughter Galeria Valeria (Aurelius Victor 40.10). Valentinian I fortified its riverbank heavily; he died in 375 in a fit of rage at Quadic envoys at Brigetio.

provinces.name: Noricum Ripense
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Pannoniae primae et Norici ripensis

phases.t: the Danube bank of Noricum with Lauriacum, Favianis and Batavis
the world of St Severinus: garrisons unpaid, towns defended by their bishops and citizens

provinces.summary: Eugippius' Life of Severinus (511) is the most vivid account of a Roman frontier province dying: unpaid soldiers walking to Italy for their wages, towns paying tribute to the Rugi, and finally Odoacer ordering the evacuation of the Roman population to Italy in 488, carrying Severinus' body with them.

provinces.name: Noricum Mediterraneum
provinces.endedNote: Frankish overlordship from c. 536-539; Slav settlement from c. 590

phases.t: inland Noricum (Carinthia)
Ostrogothic

provinces.summary: The mountain valleys of Carinthia, more sheltered than the Danube bank; Teurnia with its bishop's church became the provincial centre in the 5th century. It passed from the Ostrogoths to Frankish overlordship in the 530s and was settled by Slavs from the 590s.

provinces.name: Venetia et Histria
provinces.endedNote: Byzantine maritime Venetia and Istria still Roman in 641

phases.t: Aquileia one of the great cities of the West; its mosaic cathedral of Bishop Theodore (after 313)
Attila sacks Aquileia (452); refugees in the lagoons
Lombard invasion; Byzantine control reduced to the lagoons (Grado, later Venice) and Istria

provinces.summary: The northeastern gateway to Italy. Attila's destruction of Aquileia in 452 drove refugees into the lagoons, and Cassiodorus' letter of 537-538 to the 'tribunes of the maritime people' describes the lagoon dwellers and their salt-pans. When the Lombards entered Italy in 568 at Forum Iulii, the patriarch fled to Grado, and Byzantine Venetia began.

provinces.name: Aemilia

phases.t: the Via Aemilia from Placentia to Bononia
partly Lombard after 569; Bononia and the eastern towns held from Ravenna

provinces.summary: The towns of the Via Aemilia, many of which Ambrose described in 387 as 'corpses of half-ruined cities'. Divided between Lombards and the exarchate after 568.

provinces.name: Liguria (late, with Milan)

phases.t: Mediolanum an imperial capital (from Maximian); Constantine and Licinius' agreement at Milan (313); Ambrose bishop (374-397)
court moves to Ravenna (402); Milan sacked by the Goths in 539; Ticinum the Ostrogothic second capital
Milan taken by the Lombards (September 569)

provinces.summary: Late antique 'Liguria' was the northwest of the Po plain, not the Riviera: Milan, Ticinum, Augusta Taurinorum and Comum. Milan was the western capital for a century, the city of Ambrose and of Augustine's conversion. In 539 the Goths and Burgundians sacked it after it went over to Belisarius, killing, Procopius says, all the men.

provinces.name: Flaminia et Picenum (Annonarium)
provinces.endedNote: still Roman (exarchate) in 641; Ravenna fell to the Lombards in 751

phases.t: the Adriatic coast from Ravenna to Ancona
Ravenna the western capital (402-476), then Odoacer's and Theoderic's, then seat of the praetorian prefect
core of the exarchate (Ravenna and the Pentapolis)

provinces.summary: Honorius moved the court to Ravenna in 402, protected by marshes and with a fleet base at Classe. The province's monuments, from Galla Placidia's mausoleum to Theoderic's tomb and Justinian's San Vitale, are the best surviving ensemble of late antique art. It remained the heart of Byzantine Italy until 751.

provinces.name: Raetia Prima
provinces.endedNote: ceded to the Franks by Vitiges, 536-537
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Raetiae primae et secundae

phases.t: the Alpine Rhine and the Grisons passes
under Odoacer and the Ostrogoths (Cassiodorus' letters to the dux Raetiarum)

provinces.summary: The Alpine part of Raetia with Chur, controlling the passes between Italy and the upper Rhine. Theoderic treated it as 'the bulwark of Italy' (Variae 7.4). Vitiges ceded it to the Franks in 536-537.

provinces.name: Raetia Secunda
provinces.endedNote: Roman administration lapsed in the later 5th century
provinces.governor: praeses; dux Raetiae primae et secundae

phases.t: the Danube-Iller-Rhine frontier
Alamannic and Iuthungian pressure; Roman control fades

provinces.summary: The Bavarian plain between the Iller and the Inn behind the late Roman Danube-Iller-Rhine line, defended by Valentinian's forts. Roman authority dissolved in the later 5th century.

provinces.name: Alpes Cottiae (late, Ligurian)
provinces.endedNote: conquered by the Lombard king Rothari, c. 643
provinces.capitalName: Segusio in the 4th century; Genua the main city later

phases.t: Italian province; by the 6th century it lay along the Ligurian Apennines and coast
Genua and the Riviera held by the empire after the Lombard invasion

provinces.summary: Paul the Deacon defines the Cottian Alps as the Ligurian Apennines with Genua, Savona and Bobbio; the archbishop of Milan took refuge at Genua from the Lombards. Rothari conquered the coast around 643.

provinces.name: Tuscia et Umbria
provinces.endedNote: Perusia corridor and south Etruria still Roman in 641

phases.t: Etruria and Umbria; battle of Busta Gallorum (Taginae) in 552
mostly Lombard after c. 570; the Byzantine corridor through Perusia linked Rome to Ravenna

provinces.summary: Etruria and Umbria, the hinterland of Rome. Narses destroyed Totila at Busta Gallorum in the Apennines in 552. After the Lombard invasion only the corridor along the Via Amerina through Perusia kept Rome in contact with Ravenna.

provinces.name: Picenum Suburbicarium
provinces.endedNote: absorbed by the Lombard duchy of Spoleto, c. 570s-580s

phases.t: southern Picenum, separated from Flaminia

provinces.summary: Southern Picenum, separated from Flaminia et Picenum in the later 4th century and assigned to the vicar of Rome. Ravaged in the Gothic war (Auximum besieged 539) and absorbed by the Lombard duchy of Spoleto.

provinces.name: Campania
provinces.endedNote: Naples and the coast still Roman in 641

phases.t: the richest part of Italia Suburbicaria: Capua, Neapolis, Puteoli; Vesuvius erupts (472)
Belisarius takes Naples through an aqueduct (536); Totila retakes it (543)
inland Campania Lombard (duchy of Benevento); Naples, Cumae and the coast Byzantine

provinces.summary: The Bay of Naples remained a playground of the Roman aristocracy into the 5th century; the last western emperor, Romulus, was pensioned off to the Castellum Lucullanum at Naples in 476. Belisarius took Naples in 536 by sending men through a disused aqueduct. The duchy of Naples survived as a Byzantine enclave.

provinces.name: Samnium
provinces.endedNote: Lombard duchy of Benevento founded c. 570-571

phases.t: separated from Campania; earthquake of 346 and rebuilding

provinces.summary: The Samnite uplands, separated from Campania in the mid-4th century. Inscriptions record the rebuilding of its towns after the great earthquake of 346. It became the core of the Lombard duchy of Benevento.

provinces.name: Valeria (Italian)
provinces.endedNote: absorbed by the Lombard duchy of Spoleto, c. 570s

phases.t: the central Apennines: Reate, Nursia, Alba Fucens, Corfinium

provinces.summary: A mountain province carved from Picenum and Samnium in the later 4th century. Benedict was born at Nursia around 480. Gregory the Great's Dialogues are full of its hermits and its sufferings at the hands of the Lombards.

provinces.name: Apulia et Calabria
provinces.endedNote: the Salento ports still Roman in 641

phases.t: Apulia and the Salento (ancient Calabria)
Lombard expansion from Benevento; Tarentum, Brundisium, Hydruntum and Gallipolis remain Byzantine

provinces.summary: Grain and wool country of southeast Italy, with the Adriatic crossing at Brundisium and Hydruntum. The Salento ports remained in Byzantine hands, and the name Calabria later migrated to the toe of Italy.

provinces.name: Lucania et Bruttii

phases.t: the toe of Italy
Alaric dies at Consentia (410); Cassiodorus' Vivarium at Scyllaceum (c. 554); largely Byzantine after the Lombard advance

provinces.summary: The far south, a land of pastoralism and great estates. Alaric died at Consentia in 410 and, Jordanes says, was buried in the bed of the Busentus. Cassiodorus retired to his estate at Scyllaceum and founded the monastery of Vivarium, a key link in the copying of classical texts.

provinces.name: Africa Proconsularis (Zeugitana)
provinces.endedNote: Carthage fell to Hassan ibn al-Numan in 698
provinces.governor: proconsul (outside the vicar's authority); consularis under Justinian's prefect

phases.t: the hinterland of Carthage; Donatist schism and Augustine's polemics; Conference of Carthage (411)
Vandal invasion
Vandal kingdom; Carthage taken on 19 October 439
Justinianic province under the praetorian prefect of Africa
under the exarch of Carthage

provinces.summary: The reduced proconsular province of Carthage, still the second city of the West in 400. The Conference of Carthage (411) brought 286 Catholic and 279 Donatist bishops face to face and ended with an imperial ban on Donatism. Gaiseric's capture of Carthage in 439 was the greatest single blow to the western empire's finances.

provinces.name: Byzacena (Byzacium)

phases.t: the olive belt of southern Tunisia
Vandal; Moorish revolts from the 480s
Justinianic; Moorish wars of Solomon and John Troglita (546-548)
Arab invasion; exarch Gregory killed at Sufetula (647); Kairouan founded (670)

provinces.summary: The great olive-oil country, whose amphorae fed Rome and later Constantinople. The Moorish wars of the 540s are told in Corippus' Latin epic Iohannis. The exarch Gregory, who had rebelled against Constans II, died fighting the Arabs at Sufetula in 647.

provinces.name: Tripolitania

phases.t: the three cities (Leptis, Oea, Sabratha); Austurian raids of 363-365 and the scandal of the comes Romanus
Vandal and Moorish control
recovered by the local revolt of Pudentius (533); Amr ibn al-As takes Tripoli (643)

provinces.summary: Septimius Severus' homeland. Ammianus tells how the comes Romanus refused to defend Leptis against the Austuriani unless supplied with 4,000 camels, then covered up his failure at court. Justinian's Leptis shrank behind a new wall enclosing a fraction of the old city.

provinces.name: Mauretania Sitifensis (Mauretania Prima)

phases.t: eastern part of Caesariensis
Vandal
returned to Rome by the treaty of 442
Vandal and Moorish
Byzantine Mauretania Prima

provinces.summary: The high plains round Sitifis, separated from Caesariensis by Diocletian (the Verona List garbles its name). It changed hands repeatedly in the 5th century; under Justinian it was the westernmost securely held province of Africa.

provinces.name: Numidia Cirtensis
provinces.endedNote: reunited by c. 314; Cirta renamed Constantina

phases.t: northern, civilian Numidia

provinces.summary: One half of Diocletian's divided Numidia, attested in the Verona List. The Great Persecution's surrender of scriptures at Cirta (303), recorded in the Gesta apud Zenophilum, fed the Donatist schism.

provinces.name: Numidia Militiana

phases.t: southern, military Numidia with Lambaesis

provinces.summary: The southern half of Diocletian's Numidia, centred on the legionary base at Lambaesis. Its name advertised its military character.

provinces.name: Tarraconensis (late)

phases.t: the Ebro valley and the northeast
Bagaudae (440s-450s); last Roman province in Spain, taken by Euric (472-475)

provinces.summary: The northeast of Spain, the last part of the peninsula under Roman government. Hydatius records Bagaudic risings in the Ebro valley in the 440s-450s. Euric's generals took Pamplona, Caesaraugusta and Tarraco in 472-475.

provinces.name: Carthaginiensis
provinces.endedNote: Roman government effectively ended by c. 460 (approximate)

phases.t: the centre and southeast, including the Balearics
Balearics separated
Vandals sack Carthago Nova (425); Majorian's invasion fleet destroyed at Portus Illicitanus (460)

provinces.summary: Central and southeastern Spain. Majorian assembled his fleet here in 460 for an invasion of Vandal Africa, only to have it captured by Gaiseric through treachery. Toledo, in its interior, became the Visigothic capital, while the coast round Cartagena was Byzantine Spania from 552.

provinces.name: Gallaecia

phases.t: the northwest with its gold districts and legio VII Gemina
allotted to the Sueves and Hasding Vandals (411)

provinces.summary: The northwest, home of the ascetic movement of Priscillian, the first Christian executed for heresy (Trier, 385), and of the chronicler Hydatius, bishop of Aquae Flaviae, who recorded the Suevic kingdom that replaced Roman rule from 411.

provinces.name: Insulae Balearum

phases.t: separated from Carthaginiensis
Vandal
recovered by Apollinaris for Justinian (534); attached to Africa, later to Spania

provinces.summary: The Balearic Islands, separated from Carthaginiensis between 369 and 385. Bishop Severus' letter on the forced conversion of the Jews of Minorca (418) is a rare document of island life. They remained Byzantine long after Spania was lost.

provinces.name: Lugdunensis Prima

phases.t: Lyon, Autun, Langres, Chalon
Burgundian control from the 460s

provinces.summary: Lyon and Burgundy. Autun's panegyrics to Constantius I and Constantine (c. 297-312) are the voice of a Gallic city rebuilding after the 3rd-century crisis. The Burgundians made Lyon one of their capitals in the 460s-470s.

provinces.name: Lugdunensis Secunda
provinces.endedNote: absorbed into the Frankish kingdom by c. 486 (approximate)

phases.t: Normandy; Saxon Shore forts on the Channel coast

provinces.summary: Coastal Normandy, part of the Channel defence against Saxon raiders (the litus Saxonicum per tractum Gallicanum). Its Roman administration merged into the Frankish world by the 480s.

provinces.name: Lugdunensis Tertia
provinces.createdNote: split from Lugdunensis II in the later 4th century

phases.t: Touraine, Anjou and Armorica; the tractus Armoricanus command

provinces.summary: Tours, Angers and the Armorican peninsula. Martin, bishop of Tours (371-397), made the city the religious centre of Gaul. Armorica was repeatedly in revolt against Roman officials in the 5th century and received British settlers who made it Brittany.

provinces.name: Lugdunensis Senonia

phases.t: Sens, Paris, Orleans, Auxerre, Chartres

provinces.summary: The Paris basin. Julian was proclaimed Augustus at Lutetia in 360, and in 451 bishop Anianus held Orleans against Attila until Aetius arrived. It belonged to the realm of Aegidius and Syagrius until Clovis conquered it.

provinces.name: Belgica Prima

phases.t: Trier an imperial capital (Constantius I, Constantine, Valentinian I, Gratian)
court and prefecture leave for Italy and Arles; Trier sacked repeatedly in the 410s-440s

provinces.summary: Trier was the capital of the West for most of the 4th century, its Aula Palatina and imperial baths still standing. Ausonius' Mosella celebrates its river landscape c. 371. Salvian says Trier was sacked four times in his lifetime; Arbogast, a Frankish count of Trier, still governed it in Roman style around 470.

provinces.name: Belgica Secunda

phases.t: Reims, Soissons, Amiens, Tournai
kingdom of Aegidius and Syagrius at Soissons beside the Frankish kingdom of Tournai

provinces.summary: Reims and Soissons. The Frankish king Childeric, buried at Tournai around 481 with a Roman general's brooch and a signet ring, was in effect a federate ruler within this province. Syagrius, 'king of the Romans' at Soissons, was defeated by Clovis in 486.

provinces.name: Germania Prima
provinces.endedNote: Alamannic and Frankish control by the mid-5th century (approximate)

phases.t: the Upper Rhine frontier
Rhine crossing of Vandals, Alans and Sueves (31 December 406); Burgundian kingdom at Worms (413-436)

provinces.summary: The Upper Rhine from Mainz to Strasbourg. The great crossing of 406 began here (Jerome lists Mainz among the cities destroyed). The Burgundian kingdom at Worms, destroyed by Aetius' Huns in 436, is the historical kernel of the Nibelungenlied.

provinces.name: Germania Secunda

phases.t: the Lower Rhine; Constantine's bridge and fort at Deutz (c. 310)
Cologne taken by the Franks (355) and recovered by Julian (356)
Frankish settlement; Cologne Frankish by c. 459

provinces.summary: The Lower Rhine, where Franks had been settled within the frontier since the 3rd century. Julian's recovery of Cologne in 356 was his first success as Caesar. By the mid-5th century the city was the seat of a Rhineland Frankish king.

provinces.name: Maxima Sequanorum

phases.t: the Jura and the Swiss plateau: Besancon, Aventicum, Augusta Raurica, Vindonissa

provinces.summary: The Swiss plateau and the Jura, behind the late Roman Rhine forts from Basel to Lake Constance. Julian describes Besancon as a small town rebuilt within its old walls. The Burgundians absorbed it in the later 5th century.

provinces.name: Viennensis

phases.t: the Rhone valley: Vienne, Arles, Valence, Geneva, Grenoble
Arles seat of the prefecture of the Gauls and of the Council of the Seven Provinces (418); Burgundians take Vienne (c. 470)

provinces.summary: The Rhone valley. Arles, Constantine's favourite residence in Gaul, became the seat of the Gallic prefecture around 407, and Honorius' edict of 418 ordered an annual council of the Seven Provinces to meet there. The rival claims of the bishops of Vienne and Arles were adjudicated by Pope Leo in 450.

provinces.name: Narbonensis Prima

phases.t: Narbonne and Toulouse
Ataulf marries Galla Placidia at Narbonne (414); Toulouse the Visigothic capital (418); Narbonne surrendered to Theoderic II (462)

provinces.summary: Languedoc. Ataulf married Galla Placidia at Narbonne in January 414 in a Roman ceremony, wearing Roman dress. Toulouse became the Visigothic capital after 418, and the count Agrippinus handed Narbonne to the Goths in 462.

provinces.name: Narbonensis Secunda

phases.t: eastern Provence: Aix, Forum Iulii, Antipolis, Apt; monastery of Lerins (c. 410)

provinces.summary: Eastern Provence. The monastery founded by Honoratus on the island of Lerins around 410 produced a generation of Gallic bishops, including Hilary of Arles and Faustus of Riez. Ceded to Euric in 476.

provinces.name: Novempopulana
provinces.createdNote: by the early 4th century (Verona List: Novem populi)

phases.t: the Nine Peoples between the Garonne and the Pyrenees
partly within the Visigothic settlement of 418; Roman administration lapsed by the 470s

provinces.summary: The southwest corner of Gaul, whose separation from the Gauls was obtained by the delegate commemorated in the Hasparren inscription. Partly assigned to the Visigoths in 418.

provinces.name: Aquitanica Prima

phases.t: Bourges, Clermont, Limoges, Cahors, Rodez
Clermont, led by Sidonius Apollinaris and Ecdicius, holds out against Euric; ceded by Julius Nepos (475)

provinces.summary: The Massif Central, the land of the Arverni. Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of Clermont and son-in-law of the emperor Avitus, led its resistance to the Visigoths in 471-474, and wrote bitterly when Nepos' envoys ceded the Auvergne to Euric in 475.

provinces.name: Aquitanica Secunda

phases.t: Bordeaux, Poitiers, Saintes, Angouleme, Perigueux, Agen
assigned to the Visigoths of Wallia as federates

provinces.summary: The Atlantic southwest, a land of great villas and rhetorical schools: Ausonius, teacher of Gratian and consul in 379, came from Bordeaux. It became the core of the Visigothic federate settlement of 418, the first barbarian kingdom on Roman soil.

provinces.name: Maxima Caesariensis

phases.t: the southeast with London and the Saxon Shore forts

provinces.summary: The southeast of Britain, with London, renamed Augusta in the 4th century (Ammianus 27.8.7), seat of the vicarius. Its coast was defended by the forts of the Saxon Shore under their own count.

provinces.name: Britannia Prima

phases.t: the west: Cirencester, Gloucester, Wroxeter, Wales

provinces.summary: The west of Britain, its capital fixed by an inscription from Cirencester naming L. Septimius, governor of Britannia Prima, who restored a Jupiter column. Villa life in the Cotswolds peaked in the 4th century.

provinces.name: Flavia Caesariensis

phases.t: the east Midlands and Lincolnshire

provinces.summary: Probably the east Midlands with Lincoln, whose bishop attended the Council of Arles in 314. The name honours the Flavian dynasty of Constantius I.

provinces.name: Britannia Secunda

phases.t: the north with Hadrian's Wall

provinces.summary: The north of Britain, held by the dux Britanniarum and the garrisons of Hadrian's Wall, which the Notitia lists fort by fort. Constantine was proclaimed emperor at York in July 306.

provinces.name: Valentia

phases.t: named for Valens by Theodosius the Elder after the 'barbarian conspiracy' of 367

provinces.summary: Ammianus says Theodosius the Elder recovered a province and renamed it Valentia in honour of Valens after the barbarian conspiracy of 367-368. Its location is unknown: the Wall zone, Wales, or a renamed existing province have all been proposed.
